title: Influence
author: Robert B. Cialdini
theme: People say yes through a small set of mental shortcuts, and understanding those shortcuts helps you persuade ethically and resist manipulation.
summary: Robert Cialdini, a social psychologist, set out to understand why people agree to requests they might otherwise refuse. Alongside laboratory studies, he spent time undercover in sales training, fundraising and advertising, watching how professionals win compliance. His conclusion is that most of our decisions run on automatic shortcuts. Unable to weigh every choice carefully, we respond to certain cues almost mechanically. These shortcuts usually serve us well, but anyone who knows them can trigger them on purpose.

He groups the cues into six principles. Reciprocity is the strong urge to repay what others give us, even small or unwanted favours. It explains why free samples work and why retreating from a large request to a smaller one often wins agreement.

Commitment and consistency describes our desire to act in line with what we have already said or done. Once people take a small, public, written or effortful step, they tend to follow it with larger ones.
Social proof is the tendency to decide what is correct by watching others, especially when a situation is uncertain or the others seem similar to us.
Liking means we agree more readily with people we find attractive, familiar, similar or complimentary, and with those linked to good feelings.
Authority is our habit of deferring to titles, uniforms and expert signals, sometimes without checking whether the expertise is real or relevant.
Scarcity makes things seem more valuable when they are rare, limited in time or at risk of being lost, and competition for them sharpens desire further.
For each principle Cialdini offers a defence: not switching off the shortcuts, but noticing when a cue has been manufactured and judging the request on its merits.

For managers, the book is both a toolkit and a warning. Influence built on genuine favours, real expertise and honest evidence lasts, while tricks that exploit automatic responses damage trust once exposed.
takeaway: Learn the six triggers of compliance so you can persuade honestly and spot when someone is using them against you.

questions.q: What is Cialdini's main explanation for why people comply with requests almost automatically?
options: They are naturally lazy
They are afraid of conflict
They rely on mental shortcuts to handle a complex world
They have been trained to obey since childhood
questions.why: Cialdini argues that people use quick rules of thumb because they cannot analyse every decision in detail.

questions.q: Which principle explains why a free sample can make people more likely to buy?
options: Reciprocity
Authority
Scarcity
Social proof
questions.why: Receiving a gift creates a felt obligation to give something back.

questions.q: In the 'reject then retreat' tactic, why does a smaller request after a refused large one tend to succeed?
options: The person has forgotten the first request
The smaller request is always cheaper to fulfil
The requester has shown greater authority
The retreat feels like a concession that invites a concession in return
questions.why: Backing down is seen as a favour, so reciprocity pushes the other person to meet it halfway.

questions.q: Which kind of initial commitment does Cialdini find most likely to shape later behaviour?
options: A private, effortless thought
An active, public commitment, such as one written down
A commitment made under heavy pressure
A commitment someone else makes on your behalf
questions.why: Commitments that are active, public and effortful bind people more strongly to acting consistently with them.

questions.q: When is social proof most powerful?
options: When the situation is uncertain and the others seem similar to us
When we are experts in the subject
When we are alone and unobserved
When the decision involves very little money
questions.why: Uncertainty and similarity make people lean most heavily on what others are doing.

questions.q: Which factor is NOT one of the drivers of liking that Cialdini describes?
options: Similarity
Compliments
Strict formal hierarchy
Familiarity through repeated contact
questions.why: Liking grows from similarity, praise, contact and positive associations, not from formal rank.

questions.q: What danger does the authority principle carry?
options: People rarely respect experts
Experts always give bad advice
Titles make people distrust a message
People may defer to symbols like titles or uniforms without checking real expertise
questions.why: Surface signals of authority can trigger obedience even when the expertise is fake or irrelevant.

questions.q: According to the scarcity principle, a 'limited time only' offer works mainly because:
options: It lowers the price
Possible loss makes the item seem more valuable
It proves the product is high quality
It comes from a trusted authority
questions.why: People value things more when access to them is restricted or about to be lost.

questions.q: What general defence does Cialdini recommend against these tactics?
options: Refuse every request from strangers
Ignore all expert advice
Notice when a cue has been artificially created and judge the request on its merits
Never accept gifts of any kind
questions.why: The shortcuts are useful, so the goal is to spot manufactured triggers rather than abandon the shortcuts entirely.

questions.q: What is the book's key lesson for managers who want to influence others?
options: Use genuine favours, real expertise and honest evidence, since exploiting triggers destroys trust
Use every trigger as often as possible
Rely only on formal authority
Avoid persuasion and simply issue instructions
questions.why: Ethical influence uses the principles truthfully, while manipulation backfires once people see through it.
